analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "Thank you, Salers, and Alvers, of the Board of Education of the County of Kent. Mr. Beatty, may you continue your argument. Mr. Chief Justice, may it please the Court. To continue from yesterday, I'd like for a few minutes to discuss Reynolds v. Sims. Now, Reynolds and its companions were, of course, state legislative cases, and the cases before the Court presently involve local governmental bodies. But in our view, Reynolds was grounded on the basic principle that a citizen's vote cannot be debased or diluted in effect on the basis of where he resides, and that a touchstone of democratic government is equal representation for equal numbers of people. Now, in our view, those basic constitutional principles are just as applicable at the local level as they are at the state level. It seems to me, Mr. Justice Harlan, that at least prima facie, every time you have a situation in which a body is elected under state law by the people, and the members of that body are elected from districts, that those districts should be substantially equal in population, or that an equivalent arrangement, which would accord appropriate weight to the votes, be established. Irrespective of the government? I would think so. It seems to me that you may reach a point where some concept of de minimis is involved, but it seems to me that that's a judgment for the states and the local bodies to make. If they decide that they want to have the body elected, presumably it's supposed to represent the constituency that's electing it. Would you evaluate, for purposes of a decision, one of these issues? Would you evaluate the functions performed by the body? And if so, what criteria would you take into account? Or would you apply this to all elected bodies, regardless of what they do? For example, if they're purely advisable, number one. Number two, suppose that they're purely administrative, administrative, as distinguished from exercising legislative or quasi-legislative powers, and number three, suppose they do exercise legislative or quasi-legislative powers. I'm not suggesting those three are the right categories, but I am asking you whether you'd describe any importance to the function of the body. I think the functions are important. I think the difficulty has to do with setting up some workable criteria. How do you decide whether a body is legislative or quasi-legislative? It seems to me that a rule that would subscribe only bodies exercising something like substantial or important or basic governmental powers could be evolved, but the problem of trying to apply that rule in each individual case, it seems to me, would be a never-ending one. Well, I understand that, but I was wondering whether you had given consideration to the functional problem and what your observation would be difficult as it may be to apply it. Well, it seems to me that if the state or the local body decides that its members are going to be elected and they're going to be elected from districts, and they've made a judgment that that body is intended to be representative of the electorate, and if they feel that it's important enough to handle it that way and the people feel that it's important enough to handle it that way, then I'd be inclined to think that the court should go along with that judgment. Now, if they disagree and they want to have it appointed or they want to elect it some other way at large or whatever, then that's open to them under the way that we view these cases. That's where I was trying to get at. The position of the United States, then, is represented by you. Yes. Is that the function performed by the body is an irrelevance? Is that so? I don't want to pressure you. This isn't as, I don't think, as substantial a problem as it might first appear because, as we point out, the bodies that are elected and are elected from districts are generally those bodies that perform important, substantial governmental functions. And as you shade off into bodies at various kinds of special districts, particularly those that lack taxing power, they're generally not elected from districts anyhow. Very few of them are. Well, the Saylor's case, for example, presents a body certainly with mixed functions. It does have within some restricted perimeter taxing power and bonding power, but its functions to include some advisory functions. I don't know how one evaluates those or weighs one against the other, which is more important, but it is a mixed body. I think it's clear that the body's functions are quite limited in the Saylor's case, and we don't... The point, I gather, that my brother Fortas is suggesting my questions is this, that in Reynolds against Sims, to which you're now directing your attention, it is clear that what was there involved were representative legislative bodies. But we're now embarking into the uncharted area of many... an infinite variety of different local units with various purposes. Take, for example, a conservancy district with precise and limited powers in a certain county, let us say, where it may be of the utmost importance that each unit in that county be represented on the conservancy districts in order for it to be able to perform its precise function of allocating the water or the whatever natural resource it's concerned with. In other words, quite a different purpose from an ordinary state legislature with broad and generalized legislative power. Yes, sir, but... You're suggesting that the same Reynolds against Sims rule should inflexibly apply all the way down the line, regardless of purposes. I don't think it's so inflexible, Mr. Justice Stewart, because before it would apply, a judgment has to be made at the state or at the local level that this body will be composed of members elected or chosen in a way that would indicate that the intention is that it be a body that represents the people, that it be elected. They don't have to do it that way. They can set it up any way they want to. It's decided that the best kind of representation on this imaginary conservancy district of mine is to have one representative from each geographical unit affected for the distribution of this resource, water, regardless of how many people reside in each geographical district. Now, if that's the policy decision made, that's what's made. But you're telling us, I gather, that would be unconstitutional. When you get to a special function district, such as a conservancy or a sewerage or a drainage district, it seems to me that it isn't out of the question if a rational basis is supported by the state in setting the thing up to allow some deviations from a population basis. But it seems to me that until you reach a position in which you have a rational basis established and shown and demonstrated, then as a prima facie matter, these bodies as well as the general function bodies should be covered by the equal population principles so long as they're elected from districts. Well, I think it's a very important question on which I hope we'll have the help of the United States. You're now saying that if it's a special purpose district as I understand you, or a special purpose body elected under state law, then this court ought to take a look at whether the method provided for selecting the members of that body has a rational basis, which is a substantial modification of... I don't think it is at all. No, sir. We developed in our brief, in a section directed towards special districts, several pages of various distinctions that might be suggested or made. We say in that part of the brief that in our view, as a prima facie matter, where they're elected from districts, we feel that the principle ought to apply. What I said is that if a state in a given situation of a special function district can show that it's set up in a particular way that deviates to some extent from population because the impact of the body, what it does, relates to certain people living in one part of the area in a different way than it does to those living elsewhere, then I think that that question is open. And I don't think... Well, why wouldn't that apply to a situation, let's say, like Saylor? Let's suppose that... Let's vary the facts a little bit. Let's suppose that the county school board was supposed to be a very large county geographically and that some of the school districts, which were small in terms of population, were in remote parts of the county. And the state says that because of the difference in the problems, the school district located in a few urban centers and these remote school districts, we think we ought to have one representative from each district on the county school board. Now, is it your position that we should or we should not take that into account? I wouldn't slide that quickly into saying that they should therefore have one representative from each school district. I'm telling you what the state is, supposing that that's what the state says. Should we then evaluate whether there is or is not a justification, just as you say we should, in the case of special purpose districts? Well, I would think that if the body has, as we point out in the brief, the body has taxing power over all of the people, then it's a little bit difficult to say that they can do these things. The kind of bodies that I'm really talking about are ones that base voter qualifications on things like property ownership. Some of these districts, it seems to me, that may make some sense because the impact of their action is on people that own property and their taxing power relates to people that own property and not to the electorate generally. But I have great difficulty with the hypothetical that you pose because it seems to me that it's not a necessary conclusion that you represent each school district just because some of the school districts may have unique problems. You may ensure that some of them that have these unique problems have some representation. Well, I don't want to press any more on this line, but I want to suggest to you that there's a difference between whether the reason is valid and whether the reason is legally relevant. And you started off with an absolute proposition with respect to something like school district, which would make the reasons that the state may have for deviating from a one-man-one-vote formula make those reasons irrelevant. And then it wouldn't matter whether the reason is a good, bad, or indifferent. The state had a real question putting to you is whether there is any such thing in your judgment, in your submission to us, as a constitutionally acceptable reason for a state deviation from the one-man-one-vote rule. I think there may be some in limited situations of special function bodies. I don't think any of that is before the court presently, but obviously these decisions are going to bear upon these questions also. Where do you stand on the CFT? Pretty close to the middle. We feel that, on balance, the judgment below should be reversed. I think it's a very close question. Say reversed? Yes. Was it a pointed board? I don't think that it's fair to say that the board was appointed. The statutory scheme there says that this assembly elects the body, and the nominating arrangement is such that it follows an election sort of pattern. The people didn't elect this board? No. It's clear that people don't elect this board. I thought the school district board selected one. Sir? I thought the school district board selected one. Right. They select a representative that meets with the representatives of the other school districts and selects the five board members. Suppose this was an equalization board that was selected in this matter. Would you hold that that was under Reynolds and Sim? What kind of boards? Equalization board. Tax equalization board. It sees whether or not my taxes and yours are fair and equal. And each county assembly representative of the state assembly representative of the equalization board that fits the board to adjust taxes. Just to consider cases involving discrepancies and discriminations in taxes and whatever they have. I think probably not, because I think that as an initial matter, you question whether that board was intended to be representative of the people in the first place. And that's the difficult question, it seems to me, of the sailors' case and the election scheme that exists there. They argue that the county board is supposed to be representative of the school districts. And therefore, since there isn't any right to vote conferred by state law, the Reynolds principle doesn't apply. I think it's... Can school districts as such claim the protection of the 14th Amendment? No, they can't. I think that's quite clear. They're not persons. It seems to me there's a danger in that case. And the danger lies in sanctioning this kind of two-step election arrangement. Because I don't know what would happen if a state decided to set its state legislative apportionment up this way. Suppose a state said that each county clerk shall meet together and pick the members of the legislature. I would have some difficulty with that. I also have some difficulty distinguishing... It's slightly different, isn't it? Well, I don't know how different it is. They would be elected by the people... legislature passes the law. Ordinarily, they're elected by the people. Well, a tax board... I'm sure some states may elect them, but I don't know any of them. I think Saylor's is a close and difficult case. And we point out in our brief that if the court is concerned about the two-step election scheme that exists there, that we would submit that, nevertheless, most school boards are directly elected by the people and that they at least should be covered by the equal population principle where they're elected from districts. I thought we got into this on the proposition that it had to be an invidious discrimination, something that had no reason to it. And certainly it's reasonable for a school board to be selected like this. It's done all over the country, isn't it? Right in the district. That's where... The judges select the school board. That's where the court started, but I think that... I think the court went beyond that in Reynolds and the companion case and determined... I don't know about the courts. I still stick to the baker. Well, do you insist that... Do you insist that... for Reynolds to apply, the body must have legislative functions? I don't think so because I think it's almost impossible to decide that. You end up with... You know, you start backing off as to what it does and pretty soon you're... It seems to me... Wouldn't the principal apply to election of statewide officials? Let's say, take the treasurer of the state, hold the administrative office. I don't think that... I don't know what you mean the principal would apply. If he's elected statewide, I assume he's elected at large. Oh, he is. What if you have the... have the unit vote system? Well, I assume Gray versus Sanders takes care of that. Well, I know it takes care of it because the 14th Amendment does catch non-legislative... Yes. ...bodies or functions also. I agree with that, but as a policy matter, I think it's difficult, even if it didn't, to try to draw these lines between what at the local level is legislative and what is not. What would you say, Mr. Peter, is a system of electing judges by districts to support the statewide jurisdictions? We point out in our brief and a fairly extensive footnote that there has been some litigation involving this question. I don't think that in a general parlance, judges are intended to be representative, even if they're elected. I think this is a difficult problem. I personally would come out holding that the equal population principle does not apply. I don't understand, if you would, why you would say it does apply to bodies like tax reports and such. I don't think I would say that it would apply. No, I see. Because, as I said, it seems to me that you have to make a judgment when you get out on the extreme. I don't know. What's the criteria of the judgment? That they do or do not have legislative power? No, not that. But whether the body or the board or the office is one that is intended to be a representative office so that there is the relationship between... I don't follow. What does representative mean if it doesn't mean having some legislative power? What does it mean? Well, it seems to me that representative means that the state has made a judgment that there is the kind of relationship between the voter and the powers that the body or the person does that this person acts in some respects in the place of the individual, the voter. And I don't think we think the judges do that. and I hope we don't. And that's the way the Third Circuit came out in one of these cases. But I don't know. I think those are difficult questions and they're at the extreme of the first one. Mr. Strawacker. Mr. Chief Justice, may it please the court. There are three other cases. I believe the court is fully appraised of the, let me say, unusual circumstances, unique circumstances in the Saylor's case. I'm sure the court understands thoroughly the Constitution questions that we write. Now we have one peculiar facet. The Solicitor General says that the de facto question, which unfortunately is in our case, is constitutionally insignificant and we certainly agree. The difficulty is that the appellants have brought it here and it's one of their claims of relief that the transfer which triggered this litigation, the transfer by the Kent County Board of Education two Kentwood Public Schools and I represent a couple of public schools, is void. And the relief I ask is that this court set that transfer aside. Now that means six and a half million dollars of valuation to my school district client in a 14-room modern schoolhouse. The three judges in the district court were unanimous that at least the body was a defractive body and that the transfer should stand. Now whatever else happened in Salis in number 430, I urge the court to say that they affirm the three judges of the district court and please prevent the transfer to stand. One last word. we urge that a constitutionally apportioned legislature is more competent to determine the method of selecting its numerous diverse boards or agencies and selecting the membership of and the peculiar circumstances that may exist and change from time to time in the state than any court. Number 624, Earl C. Moody et al., Appellants versus Richmond M. Flowers et al. Mr. Ryan. Mr. Chief Justice, may it please the court. In this case, we have an appeal from a decision of a three-judge statutory court in Alabama that 19,000 residents of the county of Houston may elect four members of a five-man board board while 31,000 residents of Houston County who live in the city of Dothan can elect only one. We have a five-man board. There is a judge of probate who is elected at large and who presides over the board but he votes only in case of a tie and he's voted only once in the last seven years and so it is actually a five-man board. board. Now, this five-man board is elected from districts and those districts have been carved out so that the rural voters and on page 57 of the record we have set forth the number of qualified voters in each one of these five districts and in each one of the four that elect one man from the rural district they have a little over a thousand qualified voters that adds up to 5,700 in all. So, 5,700 electors elect four members of the board. There are 9,000 qualified voters in the city of Dothan and they elect one. So, ours has none of the two-step problems that some other cases have here. This is a classic case of malapportionment on a county level. And our position is that, as the dissenting judge said below, that Reynolds v. Sims rules this case, that the same crazy quilt which the Chief Justice found in Reynolds and which Mr. Justice Clark mentioned in Baker, the same rule stranglehold which existed in those cases on the part of the rule elements exist throughout the state of Alabama in so far as county government is concerned. Now, this is called the Board of Revenue and Control. Is that right? Yes, Your Honor, it is. And how many, is this same set up in every county in Alabama? Well, they're sometimes called county court, or commissioner courts, and the title in some instances is the same. There are 29 districts throughout the state of Alabama that are almost identical with Houston County in that they are districted and the members of the county governing board, by whatever name it's called, and they all have substantially the same power throughout the state. It's conferred by general state law. General superintendents of roads and bridges and ferries and so forth within the county? Yes, Your Honor. They have a taxing. Do they have a taxing power, too? Yes, Your Honor. They tax the whole county. Let's see, they tax the whole county just for those purposes or for general purposes? No, no. They tax them for all purposes. For example, in Houston County, it has a budget of about a million and a half on average each year. And that pays for all the people that we name in Appendix C of our brief, which is 165 people, the probate judge, tax assessor, the circuit court registers, office. They being all county employees or officials, is that it? Yes, Your Honor. And they tax county-wise. Now, one of the, I'm not arguing its constitutional significance, but it's an illustrative fact. The county has an assessed valuation of around $30 million. $21 million of that assessed valuation is in the city of Doha. So they, in effect, pay 69% of the taxes. And there are some instances of discrimination that we could point to here, but I say I'm not using those for any reason other than illustrative facts. Now, insofar as the powers of this particular county board is concerned, and I say that the powers are pretty much the same throughout the state of Alabama. It has the function in charge of public health, welfare, sanitation, hospitals, waterworks, county, or the library, all county property, including public buildings, courthouse, things like that. Does it have the power of custody and maintenance of those facilities? Yes, Your Honor. Does it have legislative power? To impose taxes and condemnation power, yes. It also has the power of airport zoning, which is certainly a legislative power. So it has certain legislative powers, and I think there's not much more important power than the power to tax all the people, all the 50,000 who live in the county, for the operation of all these county services. It has unrestricted autonomous power to impose taxation without reference to the state legislature? Oh, there are some restrictions imposed in the Constitution and statutes of Alabama, but within the areas that are laid out for all county courts or all county boards, they decide how much to tax the people of Houston County. And those taxes, I say, are collected county-wise. It has the power, for example, to issue revenue bonds, condemn property, and to impose taxes for general and special purposes. It imposes taxes for the library fund, the hospital fund, and things like that. How about laws regulating the use of the road? Are they state laws? They're state laws, your honor. No county laws as such? No. All the traffic laws as such are statewide, if that's what your honor has in mind. Does it have a power to enact ordinances? No, your honor. It does not. It's the same as municipal government would ordinarily have. No, it does not. But I think that insofar as legislative power is concerned, I say it's... Well, what's the zoning? Airport zoning is a power that was recently conferred... Is that an ordinance? I mean, it's the same for it serves the same function as an ordinance. Pardon? It serves the same function as an ordinance. In what form do they put out their zoning decisions? It would be in the form of an ordinance, yes. So I think that my answer ought to be qualified. I was just informed of this airport zoning power this morning. That's a limited zoning power, then, just airport zoning. Yes. To protect the approaches to the airport. Now, I think that the... Mr. Ryan, before you go on, would you mind stating what the limits of the tax power are? The limit is a fixed amount that is fixed by the Alabama Constitution and legislature. Isn't it, Mr. Lutton? Yes. So they can't go above that, but anything underneath that they can impose. So it's a rather broad discretionary power. And is there a limitation in terms of a description of purposes for which the taxing power may be exercised within that monetary limit? Well, there are certain things that are specified like schools, but actually they have a general taxing power for all the purposes of the county. And then they have a special taxing power for special purposes. So sometimes it's specified, as in the case of a special tax for the hospitals and schools, and the taxing resolutions are set forth in the record here, and they specify so much for schools, so much for roads and buildings, so much for this. You say they have a public health power. Could the county, for example, decide that it's going to have a new mental health facility and then levy taxes to support that? Yes, Your Honor. There's no question that they have that power. Do they have any bonding power? Yes, it has the power to issue bonds and revenue bonds particularly. So it has really very broad and very important governmental powers. Now, the same facts I say that appeared in Reynolds v. Sims, we contend, are present here. And I take it that in the light of Baker and the cases that it followed, it's not necessary for me to discuss jurisdiction generally of the district courts. That's pretty well settled in the standing of these voters to maintain this suit and their right to bring it under the Civil Rights Act. So I will not go into that subject on the jurisdiction of a district court as such. But the Solicitor General has raised a question as to the propriety of the assembling of a three-judge court in this case. He has said that the statute here involved applies only to Houston County. And he's correct. But he didn't look at the other 67 counties of Alabama and find that 61 of them have substantially the same substance power in them. The legislature has retained to itself the right to redistrict all these counties. And it has really just filled in the numbers in these other statutes. Now, there are 29 of them that elect on a district basis almost identically to that of Houston County. And when the Solicitor General raised this problem, we tried rather quickly to get the population of counties involved and the largest city. All of these have a city of some consequence. pens. And I'm afraid our first telegrams were kind of messed up by Western Union. We've been trying to get it straightened out ever since. But we have asked that there be distributed to the members of the court a chart which, I say, only has 12 illustrations of the disparity, the dilution of the city residents' votes. And one of the things that this chart indicates to the court is that many of these cities of consequence don't have even one full representative. They are, as was Houston up before, Houston County up before 1957, joined to an area adjacent to the city so they don't even have one full representative. So the percentage figures that we give here on those having less than one actually are much higher. But we believe that the picture is quite clear that malapportionment of these counties to give this rural element the stranglehold and control of county government exists throughout Alabama except in six counties where they have elections at large. Now there are 32 that elect at large, but they have local residency requirements which works out the same way because you have to live in these rural areas and the city only can have one resident elected. So we think that we have here what this court has spoken of in its decisions many times, a statewide policy of malapportionment, a crazy quilt stranglehold that exists really throughout the state of Alabama. These 12 that we give the court facts and figures on are located throughout the state of Alabama. and the statute which is involved, of course, refers to any state statute. Now we, that's the three judge statute, allows the invoking of the three judge court at any time you seek to restrain any state statute. Now we are not in disagreement with the decision of this court which say that this doesn't apply to city ordinances. It doesn't apply as in the Phillips case that we cite and the Swiss General cites to one federal dam or in the Collins case to one city street. But any time, and the language that this court uses in this decision is a statewide policy. Well, we certainly have it here and I can guarantee this court that the effect of its decision in this case is going to have a statewide effect in Alabama. And so I think that that shows that while you might have separate statutes, they all have the same substance. And we feel that under those circumstances, under the letter and intent of the three judge statute, that is a case required to be heard by three judges and properly heard by them. Now there's one other point that your cases make quite clear, and that is the relative importance of the case. Now this case is important not only to Alabama but throughout the nation because it, I say, involves direct election of a county board. And one other point I would make on the three judge court only, and that is, I agree with Judge Bryan's decision in the case from Virginia Beach, that once this court settles the law, then only a single judge is required. And I don't believe that in the light of the experience with Baker v. Carr and other cases that this court would be swamped with appeals from local government agencies. Now on the merits, I really believe that the principles have been settled by this court, and that insofar as the decision below saying that Houston County simply didn't exercise enough governmental power to invoke the one man, one principle, one book principle. But that is so wrong. I believe that all governmental powers are important, and certainly the powers that this county exercises are tremendously important. What more important than to take a man's property by condemnation or to tax it? Well, as this goes so far, Mr. Bryan, as you say, the focus is only on the fact that it's an elected agency, that we need not concern ourselves with how much in the way of powers the agency may have as long as it has some governmental powers? That is my position that it applies across the board. If you have a representative body and... Well, this word representative, what's that mean except that it's elected? Well, that means where you're elected. Does it mean more than that it's elected by the people? Elected by the people. That's all it means. And if it is, what else do you have to show? Well, I say that you don't have to show anything else. You can't dilute votes because the Constitution requires an equal vote in elections in our country, and there's no rational or logical or constitutional distinction between federal, state, and local governments. Well, then, an elect, you would apply, and the hypothetical put in the previous case, a tax equalization board that may be elected a member from each county. Yes, sir. You'd apply, since it's an elected board, although its function is only to equalize assessments among the several counties according to a common standard, you'd say that the equal population principle... I would. I can see no rational distinction. And I don't believe this is going to... How about judges? I would say there, I would not change the rule. I think we have one rule, one constitutional rule that applies to anyone... So you'd apply it to judges elected at least to a statewide court? I would. I would. I can't see any difference in principle. And I think that equality of votes is required, and I don't see how you can draw a rational distinction. Gray against Sanders involved statewide elected judges, I think, didn't it? Pardon? Didn't Gray against Sanders involve the statewide elected judges? I believe it did, yes, Your Honor. But that, of course, was a different matter. That was votes within a constituency. Yes. Within a statewide constituency. That's right. And, of course, you could have an election within a county. I thought that Reynolds against Sims involved a... Well, it clearly did involve a representative legislative assembly, did it not? Now you're twisting it to say any kind of governmental power, like power of eminent domain. I'm not trying to... Private utilities... Well, private utilities have the power of eminent domain. Well, no, I'm not... And private utilities are not elected by the people. I'm saying that a body that is elected by the people, that the votes must be substantially equal... Well, what if it's... What if a state provides that this particular body shall not be elected by the people, but shall be elected by each county? Each county shall elect a representative.
